result.backlog:
# FusionDB Commercial-Parity Backlog

## P0 — Correctness (unsound today)

**1. Commit-coupled side-index deferral (M)**
Why: trigram/HNSW mutations run inline during DML *before* OCC validation; aborted txns leave phantom index entries with no compensation path. Mechanism: buffer per-txn index deltas next to the write set; apply only after validation succeeds under the existing global commit lock; abort = drop buffer (InnoDB FTS design — zero undo logic). Move call sites `src/execution/dml/insert.rs:651/676`, `update.rs:240/292`, `delete.rs:220/245`. Also makes replica apply deterministic. Source: index-txn (Pattern 2).

**2. UNIQUE sentinel key in the write set (S)**
Why: composite unique check is an unvalidated prefix scan over row_id-suffixed keys (`composite_index.rs:709-714`), so two concurrent same-value inserts both commit. Mechanism: also write a row_id-free sentinel `prefix+value_key` (value = row_id) into `write_buffer`; exact-key OCC validation (`fusion.rs:4337-4347`) then deterministically aborts the loser — this is literally CRDB/TiDB's unique-key shape. Skip sentinel when any indexed column is NULL; tombstone on DELETE, move on UPDATE; audit single-column path `insert.rs:481-503`. Source: unique-phantom.

**3. Deterministic Raft log: replicate the OCC write set, not SQL text (L)**
Why: `apply_sql` (`store.rs:57-81`) re-executes SQL per replica — executor-generated UUIDs, NOW(), and swallowed per-statement errors guarantee divergence; no production system replicates raw SQL, and rqlite-style rewriting cannot pin executor-internal ids. Mechanism: leader executes once, captures the txn's materialized `{puts, deletes}` (+ index deltas from item 1) at commit, appends that as the Raft entry; followers apply physically, bypassing parse/OCC (proposer-evaluated KV, scaled down). Source: distributed-placement.

**4. Distributed coherence companions (M)**
Why: pgwire DML bypasses Raft entirely (two write paths → divergence even with item 3), and vote/log are in-memory (restart → double-vote / lost committed entries). Mechanism: route `pg_server` DML through `submit_raft_write` like `http_server.rs:1330`; persist vote+log under reserved FusionStorage/WAL keys; make follower apply infallible-or-halt. Source: distributed-placement.

## P1

**5. Read-path recheck: candidate-then-verify (S/M)**
Why: treating index hits as candidates verified against the base row + OCC snapshot makes residual index garbage (crashes, races, HNSW dead entries) harmless — Postgres's core invariant, defense-in-depth behind item 1. Mechanism: re-fetch row and apply snapshot visibility before returning index results; oversample/iterate when filtered (pgvector 0.8 pattern). Source: index-txn (Pattern 1) + vector-persistence.

**6. Vector index: durable-column rebuild, delta + tombstones, no graph WAL (M)**
Why: restart yields an empty index; any delete nukes the graph; dirty-flag triggers O(N) rebuild. Mechanism: (a) startup repopulation of the vectors map from persisted rows; (b) immutable built graph + brute-force delta map, background-merged past ~10k; (c) deleted-ID filter, rebuild only past ~0.2 deleted fraction (Qdrant/Milvus/LanceDB consensus). Source: vector-persistence.

**7. Batch-columnar scan kernels (L)**
Why: per-row bincode→`Vec<Value>` decode + enum dispatch dominates scan CPU; CRDB proved the fix on an identical row-KV LSM (70x micro, 4x TPC-H). Mechanism: batch (1-2k row) visitor API; decode predicate/projection columns straight into typed vectors + null bitmap + selection vector (partial decode already exists in `encoding.rs`); rewrite aggregates incl. DECIMAL fan-out as batch kernels. Source: scan-performance (Step 1).

**8. Fan-out = compute partitioning over replicated data (S)**
Why: owner-local shard semantics contradict full-keyspace Raft snapshots (double-count on merge). Mechanism: under item 3's full replication, coordinator assigns disjoint key-range slices per node; static router map becomes performance-only; preserves BENCHPROD aggregate work. Source: distributed-placement.

## P2

**9. Block-level predicate-first decode (M)** — hoist `decode_predicate_first_filtered_row` to block granularity after one LZ4 decompress + zone maps; survivor-only column decode (ClickHouse PREWHERE). Source: scan-performance (Step 2).
**10. Morsel scheduler (M)** — replace collect-then-rayon (`scan/mod.rs` ~2383) with ~100k-row work-stealing morsels; enables LIMIT early-exit, bounds peak memory. Source: scan-performance (Step 3).
**11. Adaptive filter reordering (S)** — Velox-style conjunct scoring in `scan/predicate.rs`. Source: scan-performance.
**12. Structural text-index end-state (L)** — per-SSTable immutable trigram/BM25 sidecars built at flush/compaction, or postings-as-KV; eliminates transactional index maintenance entirely. Only if items 1/5 prove insufficient. Source: index-txn (Patterns 5/6).
**13. HNSW snapshot accelerator + library swap (M/L)** — checkpoint-serialize graph + replay tail; worth it past ~1M vectors; use usearch, not unmaintained hora. Source: vector-persistence.

## Conflicts judged

- **Graph WAL**: index-txn leaves Qdrant-style WAL open "later"; vector-persistence anti-recommends any graph-mutation WAL (10x amplification; hora can't support it; vectors already durable in LSM rows). Verdict: vector-persistence wins — rebuild-from-column + snapshot (items 6/13), never a graph WAL.
- **Deferral vs sentinel**: item 1 moves index writes *out* of the write set; item 2 requires the sentinel *in* it. Not a contradiction: constraint-enforcing keys must be OCC-validated; search-index deltas must not be. Encode this distinction explicitly in the txn buffer design.
- **Sharding**: no report supports multi-raft/PD; distributed-placement sizes it as larger than all of `src/distributed/`. Verdict: full replication + compute partitioning until data exceeds one node.

## Non-goals
JIT compilation (vectorized ≈ compiled on scans; DataFusion is the Rust existence proof); rqlite-style SQL rewriting; Weaviate edge-level graph logging; multi-raft placement metadata.

reports.index-txn:
PATTERN 1 — MVCC-filtered index entries, no rollback compensation (PostgreSQL btree/GIN/GiST/pg_trgm)
- All standard Postgres index AMs insert index entries BEFORE commit and never remove them on abort. Correctness comes entirely from the heap visibility check: "A new heap entry is made before making its index entries... the index reader would be uninterested in an uncommitted row anyway"; dead/aborted entries are lazily removed — "When a heap entry is to be deleted (by VACUUM), all its index entries must be removed first." Index is a hint layer; heap is truth. Source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/index-locking.html
- So Postgres has EXACTLY FusionDB's situation (index mutated pre-commit, no compensation) and makes it safe by (a) read-time recheck against MVCC state and (b) a background reaper (VACUUM). All index page changes are additionally WAL-logged for crash redo; extensions use Generic WAL.
- GIN adds a deferred queue INSIDE the index: fastupdate pending list — "GIN is capable of postponing much of this work by inserting new tuples into a temporary, unsorted list of pending entries," merged in bulk at VACUUM / gin_clean_pending_list / size limit; searches scan pending list too. Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin-implementation.html , https://postgresqlco.nf/doc/en/param/gin_pending_list_limit/
- Applicability to FusionDB: HIGH. Cheapest fix that needs no undo logic: tag trigram postings / HNSW nodes with row key + creating txn version, and make index scans re-fetch the base row and apply the OCC snapshot check (candidate-then-verify). Aborted-txn garbage becomes harmless, cleaned by a vacuum-like sweep. FusionDB already has exact-key validation machinery; the read-path recheck also fixes the "index returns deleted rows" class of bugs.

PATTERN 2 — Deferred maintenance queue applied at commit (InnoDB fulltext) — BEST NEAR-TERM FIT
- InnoDB FTS: "updates and insertions on a full-text index are processed at transaction commit time, which means that a full-text search can only see committed data." Rollback = the buffered tokenized doc is simply discarded; there is no index compensation because nothing touched the index pre-commit. Source: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-fulltext-index.html
- Deletes are never applied to the inverted index inline: deleted DOC_IDs are logged to an FTS_*_DELETED auxiliary table and "information in the FTS_*_DELETED table is used to filter out deleted DOC_IDs" at query time; physical removal deferred to OPTIMIZE TABLE. Crash recovery: FTS_SYNCED_DOC_ID marks the flushed frontier; unsynced docs are re-parsed from the base table (rebuild-the-tail, not index WAL).
- Applicability to FusionDB: HIGHEST. FusionDB is OCC with a buffered write set + global commit lock — the deferral point already exists. Move the side-index mutations out of DML execution (currently inline at src/execution/dml/insert.rs:651/676, src/execution/dml/update.rs:240/292, src/execution/dml/delete.rs:220/245, i.e. before OCC validation) into a per-txn index-delta buffer applied only after validation succeeds (inside or immediately after the commit lock, with per-key ordering). Abort = drop the buffer; zero compensation code; also keeps Raft replicas deterministic since apply happens on the committed path.

PATTERN 3 — Rebuild-on-recovery, index never logged (Hekaton, RediSearch)
- SQL Server Hekaton: "index operations are not logged"; durability covers only data via log+checkpoint; "All indexes on memory-optimized tables are created based on the index definitions during database recovery." Sources: https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15721-f24/papers/Hekaton_SQL_Server.pdf , https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/in-memory-oltp/indexes-for-memory-optimized-tables?view=sql-server-ver17
- RediSearch 2.0: inverted index is deliberately ephemeral — only the index definition is persisted; data is re-indexed in the background on RDB/AOF load. Sources: https://redis.io/kb/doc/1pevjgdg25/where-do-indexes-reside , https://redis.io/blog/redisearch-2-0-hits-its-first-milestone/
- Applicability to FusionDB: legitimizes the current non-persisted hora HNSW for the CRASH story (rebuild from committed rows at startup is industry-sanctioned) — but it does NOT solve runtime rollback. Rebuild is only correct if the index is rebuilt from committed data; today's pre-commit mutation breaks even that invariant during runtime. Fix Pattern 2 first; keep rebuild-on-recovery as the crash answer (no WAL format work needed).

PATTERN 4 — WAL-logged index mutations (pgvector, Weaviate, Qdrant)
- pgvector piggybacks Postgres WAL/buffer manager/MVCC; the index itself is not transactionally compensated — dead tuples stay in the HNSW graph and degrade recall until VACUUM (documented recall-loss issue). Later versions added an MVCC-compliant snapshot check on index scans. Sources: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/issues/244 , https://kernelmaker.github.io/pgvector , https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md
- Weaviate runs a dedicated HNSW commit log (a WAL of graph mutations: node placements + neighbor links) replayed at startup, plus HNSW snapshots (2025) to cut replay time; its history of condensing/combining crash bugs (#1703, #4038, #8908) shows this path's maintenance cost. Sources: https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/concepts/storage , https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/configuration/hnsw-snapshots , https://github.com/weaviate/weaviate/issues/1703
- Qdrant: everything goes to a WAL first, then into segments; each point carries a version number and "if the new change has a sequential number less than the current version of the point, the updater will ignore the change" — idempotent replay without transactional index undo. Source: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/manage-data/storage/
- Applicability to FusionDB: MEDIUM/LATER. Only needed when HNSW persistence lands. If so, copy Qdrant's per-key version stamping for idempotent replay rather than Weaviate-style edge-level graph logging (highest complexity, most crash-bug surface).

PATTERN 5 — Immutable segments + tombstone/delete-bitmap filtering (Lucene/Elasticsearch, Milvus)
- ES: ops are acked only after the translog write; Lucene segments are immutable; deletes are soft-deletes; crash recovery replays translog into the index. Sources: https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/index-settings/translog , https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/29530
- Milvus: WAL-first; growing segments are brute-force searchable until sealed; deletes materialize as an in-memory bitmap applied as a filter at query time; indexes built asynchronously on sealed (immutable) segments. Sources: https://milvus.io/docs/data_processing.md , https://milvus.io/blog/2022-02-07-how-milvus-deletes-streaming-data-in-distributed-cluster.md
- Applicability to FusionDB: HIGH for trigram/BM25 given the LSM storage: build inverted/trigram sidecars per-SSTable at flush/compaction (post-commit by construction, crash-safe because flush is already ordered after WAL), brute-force or small delta-index the memtable, and filter deletes via tombstones. This ELIMINATES transactional index mutation instead of compensating it — best "good taste" option for the text indexes.

PATTERN 6 — Index entries as ordinary transactional KV (SQLite FTS5, CockroachDB)
- SQLite FTS5 stores its inverted index in shadow tables (<t>_data/<t>_idx) that are plain b-trees in the same transaction — commit/rollback/crash-safety inherited for free; integrity_check gained xIntegrity coverage for FTS5 in 3.44. Sources: https://www.sqlite.org/vtab.html , https://sqlite.work/optimizing-fts5-external-content-tables-and-vacuum-interactions/
- CockroachDB: secondary index entries are ordinary MVCC KV writes carrying write intents; on abort "the reader ignores the intent" and cleanup is lazy — index rollback is just transaction machinery. Source: https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/transaction-layer
- Applicability to FusionDB: HIGH long-term for trigram/BM25 — encode postings as FusionStorage keys (term‖rowkey → ()) so OCC/MVCC/WAL/compaction all apply automatically; no separate consistency mechanism to build. Not a fit for the HNSW graph (edges don't decompose into independent KV rows without killing search locality).

2024–2026 RESEARCH STATE (graph/vector index freshness)
- Consensus: nobody does edge-granularity transactional HNSW. State of practice is delta buffer + tombstones + background merge, read-time filtering. FreshDiskANN: in-memory short-term index + periodic merge, deletes batched and consolidated (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.09613). SPFresh (SOSP'23): in-place partition rebalancing (LIRE) for billion-scale updates (https://arxiv.org/html/2410.14452v1). 2025 follow-ups: topology-aware localized graph updates (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.00402), Ubis balanced streaming index (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.00563), P-HNSW crash-consistent HNSW on persistent memory (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/19/10554). MyRocks ships an offline PK-vs-secondary consistency checker as a safety net (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p3217-matsunobu.pdf).

CONCRETE RECOMMENDATION FOR FUSIONDB (ranked, cheap→structural)
1. Commit-coupled deferral (Pattern 2, ~small diff): collect trigram/HNSW deltas in the txn write set; apply after OCC validation under the existing global commit lock; abort drops them. Removes the rollback bug with zero compensation logic. Call sites to move: src/execution/dml/insert.rs:651/676, update.rs:240/292, delete.rs:220/245.
2. Deletes as tombstones, never inline graph unlink: query-time filter set + periodic consolidation (InnoDB FTS_DELETED / Milvus bitmap / FreshDiskANN precedent).
3. Read-path recheck (Pattern 1): index results are candidates; verify against the base row + snapshot before returning. Makes residual index garbage (bugs, races, crash) harmless — defense in depth, also fixes HNSW dead-entry recall skew.
4. Crash story: keep rebuild-on-recovery for both in-memory indexes (Hekaton/RediSearch precedent); optional snapshot file later for startup time (Weaviate HNSW snapshots).
5. Structural end-state for text indexes: per-SSTable immutable trigram/BM25 sidecars built at flush/compaction (Pattern 5) or postings-as-KV (Pattern 6) — deletes transactional index maintenance from the design entirely.
reports.unique-phantom:
## UNIQUE Enforcement in KV/OCC Engines Without Gap Locks — Research + FusionDB Applicability

### How production systems do it

**CockroachDB — row_id-free index key IS the sentinel + ConditionalPut**
- Unique secondary indexes encode only the indexed columns into the KV key; the non-indexed PK columns are "relegated to KV values so that the KV layer detects constraint violations." Non-unique indexes append the PK to the key. So two rows with the same unique value map to the *same* KV key by construction — collision detection is delegated entirely to the KV layer. Source: https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/master/docs/tech-notes/encoding.md
- Write path uses `ConditionalPut` (fail if a value already exists at that key) instead of `Put`, catching already-committed duplicates without a separate read; concurrent writers lay write intents on the same key, so intent/timestamp conflict resolution serializes them. Source: https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/unique , https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/110873 (unique constraints *without* a backing index need an explicit search — the fallback, treated as the expensive path)
- NULL handling: NULL ≠ NULL, so rows with an indexed NULL can't violate uniqueness; CRDB appends PK to the key *only for those rows* (stored in both key and value) so they remain distinct KV keys. Source: encoding.md above.

**TiDB/TiKV (Percolator-style) — same key shape, conflict at prewrite**
- Unique index: `Key: tablePrefix{TableID}_indexPrefixSep{IndexID}_indexedColumnsValue`, `Value: RowID`. Non-unique index puts `_{RowID}` in the key. Source: https://docs.pingcap.com/tidb/stable/tidb-computing/
- Optimistic transactions defer the constraint check to COMMIT: prewrite on the exact unique-index key aborts if it finds a lock or a write record with `commit_ts > start_ts` ("already-exist error" returned in the prewrite phase). `tidb_constraint_check_in_place` opts into check-at-execution instead. Sources: https://docs.pingcap.com/tidb/stable/constraints/ , https://docs.pingcap.com/tidb/stable/optimistic-transaction/ , https://tikv.org/deep-dive/distributed-transaction/percolator/
- Net: Percolator never needs predicate validation for uniqueness because the unique key excludes RowID — write-write conflict on the exact key is sufficient.

**FoundationDB / Record Layer — the one system that solves it with range validation instead**
- Record Layer appends the PK to *all* index entries (even unique ones); uniqueness (`UNIQUE_OPTION` → `RecordIndexUniquenessViolation`) is sound because FDB's resolver validates read **conflict ranges**, not exact keys: the uniqueness check range-reads the indexed-value prefix, and any concurrent committed write intersecting that range aborts the transaction at commit. Sources: https://foundationdb.github.io/fdb-record-layer/Overview.html , https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/developer-guide.html , https://javadoc.io/static/org.foundationdb/fdb-record-layer-core/2.10.164.0/com/apple/foundationdb/record/metadata/IndexOptions.html , https://www.foundationdb.org/files/record-layer-paper.pdf
- The paper explicitly warns that hand-rolled manual conflict ranges are bug-prone and should be encapsulated in index abstractions. Forum discussion of the exact prefix-read-conflict-range uniqueness pattern: https://forums.foundationdb.org/t/questions-regarding-fdb-transaction-conflict-on-two-concurrent-transactions/2913

**Taxonomy**: (a) sentinel/shared-key collision (CRDB, TiDB — key excludes row id, value carries it); (b) write-intent/lock on the unique key itself (Percolator prewrite — same key shape, pessimistic detection); (c) predicate/range read validation (FDB — only sound if the OCC validates ranges). Nobody uses gap locks in this class of system; (a)+(b) are the same idea at different phases.

### FusionDB code grounding (verified in-repo)

- OCC commit validation is **write-set only, exact-key, first-committer-wins** under the global commit lock: `/root/FusionDB/src/storage/fusion.rs:4337-4347` — for each `write_buffer` key, abort if `latest_committed_timestamp(key) > read_ts`. Reads (including prefix scans) are never validated.
- Composite unique check is a prefix scan: `validate_composite_unique_constraints` at `/root/FusionDB/src/execution/composite_index.rs:1075`; the entry key appends row_id: `composite_index_entry_key = prefix + value_key + ":" + row_id` at `/root/FusionDB/src/execution/composite_index.rs:709-714`. Two concurrent inserts of the same value therefore write *different* keys and the unvalidated prefix read lets both commit — race confirmed exactly as stated.

### Verdict on the proposed fix

- **Yes — writing a row_id-free sentinel key into the write set is the minimal sound fix, and it is precisely the CRDB/TiDB mechanism** (their unique index key *is* the sentinel). Because FusionDB validates the write set exact-key under the global commit lock, two concurrent txns both writing sentinel `prefix + value_key` collide deterministically: the winner commits at `commit_ts > loser.read_ts`; the loser's validation of that exact key fails. No read-set validation needed: the existing prefix read handles duplicates already committed as of `read_ts`; the sentinel write serializes concurrent writers of the same value. The commit lock makes validate-then-publish atomic, so there is no TOCTOU.
- **Soundness conditions** (all required):
  1. Sentinel must be a **write** (reads are not validated); store `row_id` as its value (enables future point-lookup check).
  2. Byte-canonical `value_key` encoding for equal values — already holds since the same encoder feeds the prefix scan; keep separator-escaping so distinct values can't alias.
  3. **Skip the sentinel when any indexed column is NULL** (SQL allows repeated NULLs; mirrors CRDB's NULL carve-out).
  4. Maintain on DELETE (tombstone the sentinel — tombstones still bump `latest_committed_timestamp`, so concurrent delete-vs-insert aborts conservatively, which is correct under SI) and on UPDATE that changes the unique columns (delete old sentinel + write new).
  5. Intra-transaction duplicates: two inserts of the same value in one txn just overwrite the sentinel in `write_buffer` — keep the existing read-your-own-writes prefix check (or probe `write_buffer` for the sentinel) to catch these.
- **Cost**: +1 KV write per row per unique index (identical to CRDB/TiDB overhead); false aborts on concurrent same-value delete+insert pairs (retry succeeds) — standard first-committer-wins behavior.
- **Cleaner long-term shape** (non-minimal): drop the row_id suffix entirely and make the sentinel *the* index entry (`key = prefix + value_key`, `value = row_id`, NULL rows fall back to suffixed keys) — halves unique-index writes and turns the duplicate check into a point read, but changes on-disk format and every lookup path; do as a follow-up, not the fix.
- **Rejected alternative**: FDB-style range read-conflict validation is more general (would also close phantom holes in FK/other predicate checks) but requires tracking range read sets and range-vs-write intersection at commit — a storage-engine-level change, not minimal.
- **Audit item**: single-column UNIQUE path (`/root/FusionDB/src/execution/dml/insert.rs:481-503`) uses the same read-then-write pattern; verify whether its index key embeds row_id and apply the same sentinel if so.
reports.vector-persistence:
RESEARCH FINDINGS: vector index durability + MVCC integration (2025-2026 practice)

**pgvector (tightest MVCC integration; per-insert WAL of graph pages)**
- HNSW inserts are crash-safe via PostgreSQL generic WAL records: `AddElementOnDisk()` wraps element-page + neighbor-page writes in one `GenericXLogStart/RegisterBuffer/Finish` unit; `UpdateNeighborOnDisk()` likewise WAL-logs neighbor rewires. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pgvector/pgvector/master/src/hnswinsert.c
- Initial index build skips WAL entirely, then logs all pages once at the end (parallel builds excepted) — bulk-build-then-log is the standard cheap pattern. Sources: https://deepwiki.com/pgvector/pgvector/5.1-hnsw-index, https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/blob/master/README.md
- Rollback/delete never touch the graph inline: dead TIDs stay in the graph; MVCC visibility is enforced at scan time by the heap visibility check (index returns candidates, heap filters invisible tuples). VACUUM does a 3-pass repair: (1) find deleted elements, (2) re-find neighbors for affected elements and swap entry point to `highestPoint` if it died, (3) mark `etup->deleted=1`, zero vector data, invalidate links. Source: https://deepwiki.com/pgvector/pgvector/7.2-index-maintenance-and-vacuum, https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/issues/824
- Filtering + dead tuples cause under-fetch; fixed in 0.8.0 with iterative index scans (`hnsw.iterative_scan`, capped by `hnsw.max_scan_tuples`) — keep walking the graph until the post-filter LIMIT is satisfied. Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/pgvector-080-released-2952/, https://docs.pgedge.com/pgvector/v0-8-0/iterative-index-scans/
- Known cost: WAL amplification (2KB vector → 20KB+ WAL from neighbor-page churn). Source: https://docs.vectorchord.ai/faqs/comparison-pgvector.html

**Qdrant (WAL of raw ops + per-segment immutable HNSW rebuilt by optimizer — no graph WAL at all)**
- All writes go to an operations WAL first (the only fsync on the hot path), then applied to segments; startup recovery = replay WAL, with per-point version numbers so stale ops are ignored idempotently. Sources: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/manage-data/storage/, https://system-design.space/en/chapter/qdrant-overview/
- Segments: appendable segments use a flat/brute-force index + mutable storage; sealed segments are immutable except tombstone deletions. The indexing optimizer builds HNSW only when a segment exceeds `indexing_threshold` (default 10k vectors); HNSW graph can be mmapped via `hnsw_config.on_disk`. Sources: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/manage-data/storage/, https://fossies.org/linux/qdrant/config/config.yaml
- Deletes are tombstone marks filtered at search time; the vacuum optimizer rebuilds a segment (copy-on-write, from stored full-precision vectors) only when deleted fraction > `deleted_threshold` (default 0.2). The HNSW graph itself is never incrementally repaired — it is rebuilt per-segment, but segments bound the rebuild cost. Sources: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/optimizer/, https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/issues/7147
- Snapshots (tar of segments + WAL) exist for backup/shard transfer, not for routine recovery. Source: https://deepwiki.com/qdrant/qdrant/8-snapshots-and-recovery

**Milvus (index fully decoupled from durability; brute-force window over fresh data)**
- Durability = WAL/streaming log + columnar binlogs flushed to object storage at segment seal; index artifacts (HNSW/IVF) are built asynchronously by index nodes AFTER seal and persisted to object storage as separate artifacts. Growing (unsealed) segments are searched brute-force; results merged with sealed-segment index results. Deletes go to delta binlogs (tombstones), physically removed by background compaction. Recovery replays WAL + reloads binlogs/index files; the index is never rebuilt from scratch on restart. Sources: https://milvus.io/docs/data_processing.md, https://milvus.io/blog/deep-dive-4-data-insertion-and-data-persistence.md

**Weaviate (the one system that WALs the graph itself)**
- HNSW has a dedicated commit log (WAL) per index containing "only the result of index calculations" (node placements + neighbor links, not the search work); startup replays it; a background process condenses/compacts commit logs by dropping redundant entries. Source: https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/concepts/storage
- Replay was too slow at 10-100M+ vectors, so v1.31 added HNSW snapshots (point-in-time serialized graph + replay of only the commit-log delta), enabled by default in v1.36; snapshot triggers: startup-with-changes, or ≥6h + ≥1 new log + delta ≥5% of snapshot size. This snapshot+delta-log design is the current SOTA answer to "WAL-coupled insert log + snapshot serialization". Sources: https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/configuration/hnsw-snapshots, https://weaviate.io/blog/weaviate-1-36-release, https://github.com/weaviate/weaviate/issues/7189
- Deletes = tombstones cleaned by periodic async cycles (`cleanupIntervalSeconds`, `TOMBSTONE_DELETION_*` knobs); high-frequency delete/update workloads remain a known pain point (repair cost, long post-reboot cleanups). Sources: https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/config-refs/indexing/vector-index, https://github.com/weaviate/weaviate/issues/3947, https://github.com/weaviate/weaviate/issues/8914

**LanceDB (lazy/delta indexing over a persisted, versioned vector column)**
- Indexes live in the versioned Lance columnar format; new rows are simply unindexed until `optimize()` delta-merges them into the existing index (no full rebuild); queries always combine index results with brute-force over unindexed rows (skippable via `fast_search=true`); `index_stats()` exposes unindexed-row count. Cloud/Enterprise automates the reindex cadence; OSS is manual. Sources: https://docs.lancedb.com/indexing/reindexing, https://lancedb.com/documentation/guides/indexing/vector-index/ (via https://lancedb.com/docs/indexing/vector-index/), https://sprytnyk.dev/posts/running-lancedb-in-production/

**FusionDB current state (verified in /root/FusionDB/src/storage/vector_index.rs)**
- `HnswIndexWrapper` already holds the full raw vector set in `vectors: HashMap<String, Vec<f32>>` beside the hora `HNSWIndex`; any upsert sets `dirty=true`; any `remove_vector` nukes `self.index = None`; `ensure_built()` rebuilds the ENTIRE graph from the HashMap on the next search (lines 46-96). Nothing is persisted; the map is repopulated only by DML, so restart = empty index until re-fed. No transactional hook: index mutation happens on execution, so an aborted OCC transaction leaves phantom vectors with no compensation.
- hora supports `dump()`/`load()` binary serialization of a built HNSW, but the project has been effectively unmaintained since ~2021-2023 — building durability features on it is a liability. Sources: https://github.com/hora-search/hora/blob/main/src/core/ann_index.rs, https://users.rust-lang.org/t/announcing-hora-0-1-0-an-approximate-nearest-neighbor-search-algorithm-library-in-rust/62993

**APPLICABILITY JUDGMENT — cheapest credible path for FusionDB**
- Verdict: lazy rebuild from the persisted vector column, NOT a WAL-coupled graph insert log. Rationale: (a) FusionDB's vectors are already durable in LSM rows behind the existing segmented WAL — vector DATA durability is solved; only index reconstruction cost and consistency are open. (b) A Weaviate-style graph commit log requires an incrementally updatable graph with stable node IDs, deletion support, and WAL hooks — hora has none of these, so that path implies replacing the ANN library first (big-bang). (c) Qdrant/Milvus/LanceDB all demonstrate that "index = disposable cache over durable column, rebuilt lazily/asynchronously" is production-credible; pgvector is the only per-insert-WAL design and pays 10x WAL amplification for it.
- Concrete staged plan (each step small, backward compatible):
  1. **Startup repopulation** (fixes "rebuilt from nothing"): on index open, scan the persisted vector column into `vectors` map; keep lazy `ensure_built()` for the graph. Zero new formats.
  2. **Kill full-rebuild-on-dirty** (LanceDB/Milvus pattern): keep the built graph immutable; add a small `delta: HashMap` of unindexed upserts searched brute-force and merged with graph results (oversampling already exists via `ANN_OVERSAMPLING_FACTOR`); background-merge into a new graph when delta exceeds a threshold (Qdrant default analog: 10k).
  3. **Tombstones instead of `index = None` on delete** (Qdrant pattern): filter a deleted-ID set at search; trigger background rebuild only when deleted fraction > ~0.2.
  4. **MVCC fix without rollback compensation**: stop mutating the index during transaction execution; apply index upserts/deletes post-commit from the committed write batch (index is a cache of committed state only — matches OCC's commit-lock point). For snapshot reads, verify each candidate's row visibility against MVCC before returning (pgvector's heap-check pattern) and iterate/oversample when filtered (pgvector 0.8.0 iterative-scan pattern).
  5. **Optional startup accelerator** (Weaviate snapshot pattern): serialize the built graph at checkpoint (hora `dump()`, or bincode of the vectors map) + replay only post-checkpoint rows from the column. Defer; only worth it past ~1M vectors where rebuild latency hurts.
- If/when the library is swapped: usearch (Rust bindings, maintained) gives serialization, memory-mapped serving via `view()`, on-the-fly deletion, and predicate-filtered search — it would make steps 3/5 native and unlock Qdrant-style mmap on_disk graphs. Sources: https://github.com/unum-cloud/USearch, https://docs.rs/usearch/latest/usearch/
- Anti-recommendation: do NOT WAL individual graph mutations through FusionDB's group-commit WAL — pgvector shows neighbor-rewire logging costs ~10x write amplification, and Weaviate needed snapshots anyway because pure log replay doesn't scale; FusionDB would pay both costs for no durability gain over the already-persisted vector column.

All research and code verification complete. Synthesizing findings.

## Statement replication vs deterministic mutation replication

- **Raft's core contract requires a deterministic state machine**: replicas converge only if every node applies identical commands with identical effects; the Raft paper's persistent-state rules (currentTerm, votedFor, log[]) and determinism assumption are foundational (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf). FusionDB violates both: `apply_sql` in `/root/FusionDB/src/distributed/store.rs:57-81` re-parses and re-executes raw SQL text per replica, and vote/log/membership/snapshot live in in-memory fields (`vote: Option<Vote>`, `log: BTreeMap` at store.rs:31-36) — restart loses votedFor (double-vote → dual-leader risk) and unsnapshotted committed entries.
- **MySQL is the canonical documentation of why raw-SQL replication breaks**: UUID(), UUID_SHORT(), RAND(), SYSDATE(), FOUND_ROWS(), ROW_COUNT(), USER() etc. are flagged "unsafe" for statement-based binlog because they yield different values on replicas; NOW() only works because MySQL smuggles the master's timestamp into the binlog event and replays it (SET TIMESTAMP); MIXED mode auto-downgrades unsafe statements to row-based events (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication-rbr-safe-unsafe.html, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/mysql-replication-excerpt/5.7/en/replication-features-functions.html). Applicability: FusionDB has no equivalent of "session context replay" — every non-deterministic expression diverges silently.
- **rqlite = the closest existing system to FusionDB's current design** (single global Raft group, SQL text in the log, full re-execution per node). Its mitigation is statement rewriting at the receiving node before the log append: RANDOM() → concrete integer, RANDOMBLOB(N) → literal blob, `now` time refs → concrete timestamp (added only in v7.7.0). Documented holes: RANDOM() in ORDER BY not rewritten, `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` column defaults not handled — users told to pass explicit values (https://rqlite.io/docs/api/non-deterministic/, https://github.com/rqlite/rqlite/blob/master/DOC/NON_DETERMINISTIC_FUNCTIONS.md). **Applicability judgment: rewriting alone cannot fix FusionDB** — its diverging UUID row-ids are generated inside the executor during INSERT, not present in the SQL text, so no text rewrite can pin them; the executor would have to pre-assign ids at the proposer anyway.
- **dqlite shows the physical alternative at the same scale**: instead of SQL text it replicates SQLite WAL frames (modified pages) through the Raft log via a custom VFS; only the leader may produce frames; explicitly advertised as "doesn't require statements to be deterministic (e.g. you can use time())" (https://canonical.com/dqlite/docs/explanation/replication, https://canonical.com/dqlite/docs/explanation/faq). Trade-off: more bytes on the wire than SQL text. rqlite v8 also moved to controlling the SQLite WAL for snapshotting (https://philipotoole.com/how-and-why-rqlite-takes-control-of-the-sqlite-write-ahead-log/).
- **CockroachDB's "proposer-evaluated KV"** is the same idea one level up: SQL is evaluated once on the leaseholder, and what enters the Raft log is the resulting low-level KV write command, so "all commands produce deterministic results so that the range replicas keep consistent states" (https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/docs/design.md, https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/master/docs/tech-notes/life_of_a_query.md, https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/replication-layer). No production distributed SQL engine replicates raw SQL text without rewriting.

## Per-range Raft groups and leaseholder routing (CRDB / TiDB / Yugabyte)

- **CockroachDB**: keyspace split into ranges; each range is its own Raft group (multi-raft); one replica holds the **lease** and is the only replica that serves consistent reads or proposes writes; leaseholder reads bypass Raft entirely; leaseholder is co-located with the Raft leader via leader leases (https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/replication-layer, https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/reads-and-writes-overview). Routing: two-level meta ranges (meta1→meta2→range descriptors) that are themselves ordinary replicated ranges; gateway's DistSender splits BatchRequests, tries the cached leaseholder first, retries transparently on NotLeaseHolder errors (https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/distribution-layer). Key point vs FusionDB: **shard metadata is consensus-replicated data, not static config**.
- **TiDB/TiKV**: data in Regions; each Region's replicas form a Raft group; Placement Driver (PD) is a separate consensus service holding all region metadata, doing placement/rebalancing and TSO (https://www.pingcap.com/blog/design-and-implementation-of-multi-raft/, https://pingcap.medium.com/a-deep-dive-into-tikv-b27989993d19). Reads: leader Lease Read (time-bounded lease avoids Raft round trip), ReadIndex for correctness, and Follower Read where a follower asks the leader for the commit index and waits to apply up to it before serving (https://tikv.org/blog/lease-read/, https://docs.pingcap.com/tidb/stable/follower-read/, https://tikv.org/blog/how-tikv-reads-writes/).
- **YugabyteDB**: tables auto-sharded into tablets; per-tablet Raft group (RF-1 followers); leader leases (~2s default) let the leader serve reads with no quorum round trip; new leader can't serve reads until it acquires the lease, closing the stale-read window under partition (https://www.yugabyte.com/blog/low-latency-reads-in-geo-distributed-sql-with-raft-leader-leases/, https://docs.yugabyte.com/stable/architecture/docdb-replication/raft/, https://docs.yugabyte.com/stable/architecture/transactions/single-row-transactions/).
- **Applicability judgment**: multi-raft requires per-group heartbeat multiplexing, consensus-backed placement metadata (meta ranges/PD), split/merge, lease management, and rebalancing — a PD-like subsystem alone is bigger than FusionDB's whole `src/distributed/` (1,353 lines). Disproportionate for a small system.

## FusionDB code facts verified (beyond the prompt's claims)

- `pg_server.rs` contains **zero** raft references — pgwire DML commits directly to local storage, never entering the log; only `http_server.rs:1330-1335` gates writes via `sql_requires_raft_write` → `submit_raft_write`. Two write paths, one replicated, one not → guaranteed divergence even with a deterministic log.
- `apply_sql` (store.rs:68-76) **swallows per-statement errors** into the response string and keeps applying — a statement can fail on one replica (e.g., OCC conflict with a local pgwire write) and succeed on another, a second divergence vector independent of non-determinism.
- Follower apply re-runs the **full OCC commit path** (parse → plan → validate → commit lock), so replication throughput is bounded by re-execution, and replica-local conflicts can abort committed log entries.
- `ShardRouter` (sharding.rs:51-79) is built once from static TOML config; round-robin `shard_id % nodes.len()` assignment; no epoch/version, no rebalance, no consensus on the map; `/raft/shards` merely describes config. Meanwhile Raft snapshot install (`replace_visible_storage`, store.rs:138-167) wipes and replaces the **entire keyspace** — i.e., the Raft layer is architecturally full-replication while the fan-out layer assumes disjoint owner-local data: with Raft on, fan-out merge double-counts; with owner-only writes, the Raft snapshot is wrong. The two subsystems contradict each other today.
- `raft_query` (api.rs:210-256) already supports optional linearizable reads via openraft `ensure_linearizable()` (ReadIndex) — the read side of model (a) already exists.

## Verdict: minimal coherent target = (a) single-raft full replication with a deterministic mutation log

- **Choose (a).** Rationale from the code: everything already built points at full replication — full-keyspace snapshot build/install, leader forwarding of writes, ReadIndex reads. Option (b) (owner-local shards, no raft for data) discards fault tolerance entirely (owner dies → shard lost), makes the existing snapshot/forwarding machinery dead code, and still needs consensus for the shard map to survive membership change — so (b) doesn't actually remove the consensus requirement, it just removes redundancy. At 228k rows / single-digit nodes, full replication cost is trivial and per-shard raft groups (mini-multi-raft) would import the CRDB/TiKV metadata problem with none of the payoff.
- **Deterministic log format: replicate the OCC write set, not SQL text.** Leader executes the statement locally through the existing executor, captures the transaction's materialized put/delete set at commit (the OCC transaction already builds exactly this before validation), and appends `{puts: [(k,v)], deletes: [k]}` as the Raft entry; followers apply the batch physically to storage, bypassing SQL, parse, OCC, and all non-determinism (UUID row-ids, NOW(), RANDOM(), error asymmetry) categorically. This is proposer-evaluated KV (CRDB) / frame replication (dqlite) scaled down. rqlite-style SQL rewriting is strictly worse for FusionDB because its UUIDs are executor-internal, invisible to a text rewriter.
- **Companion fixes required for coherence** (in priority order): (1) route pgwire DML through the same `submit_raft_write` gate as HTTP — one write path; (2) persist Raft vote + log (at minimum votedFor; reuse FusionStorage/WAL under reserved keys) — Raft safety demands durable persistent state (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf); (3) apply must be infallible or halting — a follower failing to apply a committed write batch is a fatal invariant break, not a string in a response; (4) reads stay leader-local by default with the existing `ensure_linearizable` opt-in, matching Yugabyte/TiKV lease-read semantics without implementing leases.
- **Fan-out disposition under (a)**: since every node holds all data, redefine shard "ownership" as compute partitioning — the coordinator assigns each node a disjoint key-range/hash slice of the fully replicated dataset to scan/aggregate, then merges. Routing stays config-static (acceptable because it no longer determines data placement, only work placement; a wrong map costs performance, not correctness). This preserves the existing fan-out merge code and BENCHPROD aggregate work while removing the correctness contradiction. True owner-local placement (model (b) / multi-raft) becomes a later phase only if dataset size ever exceeds a single node.

Sources: [Raft paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) | [MySQL unsafe statements](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication-rbr-safe-unsafe.html) | [MySQL replication of system functions](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/mysql-replication-excerpt/5.7/en/replication-features-functions.html) | [rqlite non-deterministic functions](https://rqlite.io/docs/api/non-deterministic/) | [rqlite NON_DETERMINISTIC_FUNCTIONS.md](https://github.com/rqlite/rqlite/blob/master/DOC/NON_DETERMINISTIC_FUNCTIONS.md) | [dqlite replication](https://canonical.com/dqlite/docs/explanation/replication) | [dqlite FAQ](https://canonical.com/dqlite/docs/explanation/faq) | [rqlite WAL control](https://philipotoole.com/how-and-why-rqlite-takes-control-of-the-sqlite-write-ahead-log/) | [CRDB replication layer](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/replication-layer) | [CRDB distribution layer](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/distribution-layer) | [CRDB reads/writes overview](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/reads-and-writes-overview) | [CRDB design.md](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/master/docs/design.md) | [CRDB life of a query](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/master/docs/tech-notes/life_of_a_query.md) | [TiKV multi-raft](https://www.pingcap.com/blog/design-and-implementation-of-multi-raft/) | [TiKV lease read](https://tikv.org/blog/lease-read/) | [TiKV reads/writes](https://tikv.org/blog/how-tikv-reads-writes/) | [TiDB follower read](https://docs.pingcap.com/tidb/stable/follower-read/) | [TiKV deep dive](https://pingcap.medium.com/a-deep-dive-into-tikv-b27989993d19) | [Yugabyte leader leases](https://www.yugabyte.com/blog/low-latency-reads-in-geo-distributed-sql-with-raft-leader-leases/) | [Yugabyte Raft docs](https://docs.yugabyte.com/stable/architecture/docdb-replication/raft/) | [Yugabyte single-row txns](https://docs.yugabyte.com/stable/architecture/transactions/single-row-transactions/)

# Closing the single-node OLAP/scan gap — research findings for FusionDB

## State of practice (2024–2026) applied to a Vec<Value> row-KV engine

The three engines most architecturally comparable to FusionDB that closed this exact gap are **CockroachDB** (row-KV on Pebble LSM → vectorized), **TiKV coprocessor** (row-KV on RocksDB → chunked/vectorized pushdown), and **DuckDB/Velox/ClickHouse** as the technique reference implementations. All converged on the same playbook: batch-columnar execution at the scan boundary, late materialization of non-predicate columns, and morsel-granular parallelism — and explicitly **not** JIT compilation.

## Step 1 (highest leverage): Batched columnar execution at the scan boundary (CockroachDB pattern)

- **Technique**: After the LSM range-merge produces KV pairs, decode rows into fixed-size typed column batches (1024–2048 rows: DuckDB `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE`=2048; ClickHouse blocks up to 65,536) — typed vectors (`Vec<i64>`, `Vec<f64>`, dictionary-encoded strings) + null bitmap + selection vector — then run filter/aggregate kernels as tight loops over typed slices instead of per-row `Value` enum dispatch. Sources: https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/how-we-built-a-vectorized-execution-engine/ , https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/internals/vector , https://clickhouse.com/resources/engineering/vectorised-query-execution
- **Evidence it works on a row-KV LSM specifically**: CockroachDB kept its row-oriented KV format and paid the row→column conversion cost at scan time — still got up to 70x CPU-time microbenchmark wins, 40x on hash join, 4x end-to-end TPC-H (https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/vectorized-hash-joiner/ , https://dev.to/jordanlewis/vectorized-sql-in-cockroachdb-nhb). TiKV did the same with `ChunkedVec` in its coprocessor (Arrow-like TiDB Chunk format): https://tikv.github.io/tikv-dev-guide/understanding-tikv/coprocessor/intro.html , https://github.com/tikv/tikv/issues/7724
- **Why this beats per-row interpretation**: amortizes dispatch overhead, enables autovectorization/SIMD, keeps working set in L1/L2 — the canonical argument from MonetDB/X100 onward; batch model is the core of ClickHouse's speed (https://clickhouse.com/resources/engineering/vectorized-query-execution).
- **Applicability to FusionDB — CONFIRMED HIGH**: I inspected the code. `src/execution/query/column_scan.rs` aggregates call `visit_row` → `RowDecoder::decode` (bincode → `Vec<Value>`) → `apply_column_aggregate_matched_row` per row, i.e. per-row allocation + enum-match dispatch, exactly the anti-pattern these systems removed. Concrete move: change the SSTable/memtable visitor API from per-(key,value) callback to per-batch, decode predicate/projection columns **directly into typed column builders** (skipping `Value` materialization for fixed-width types — bincode `decode_column`/`decode_partial` in `src/common/encoding.rs` already prove partial decode is feasible), and rewrite the existing hand-rolled aggregates (SUM/COUNT/MIN/MAX/AVG incl. the new DECIMAL fan-out paths) as batch kernels. CockroachDB's experience says the row→batch conversion cost is dwarfed by the interpretation savings. This is the single biggest expected win at 228k-row scans.

## Step 2: PREWHERE-style late materialization + projection pushdown into the block layer

- **Technique**: Evaluate predicate columns first over a whole block, produce surviving row positions (selection vector), then decode/fetch the remaining SELECT columns only for survivors. ClickHouse PREWHERE does mark-level skip + survivor-only column reads (https://clickhouse.com/docs/optimize/prewhere); its 2025 "lazy materialization" work defers row assembly past filters/TopN — on 1-in-1000 selectivity it cuts downstream column work ~1000x (https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-gets-lazier-and-faster-introducing-lazy-materialization). Foundational: Abadi et al., Materialization Strategies in a Column-Oriented DBMS, ICDE'07 (http://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadiicde2007.pdf); Velox "lazy vectors" populate only on first use (https://users.cs.utah.edu/~pandey/courses/cs6530/fall22/papers/velox/p1030-pedreira-cr2.pdf).
- **LSM-specific evidence**: LSM-OPD (arXiv 2025, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.11862) pushes filter/aggregate operators into RocksDB's compressed block scan path — direct computing on compressed blocks, avoiding full decompress+decode — showing operator pushdown below the iterator is viable in a production LSM.
- **Applicability to FusionDB — HIGH, builds on existing code**: `scan/mod.rs` already has `decode_predicate_first_filtered_row` (decode predicate columns, then full row) — the row-granular version of this idea. Next increment: hoist it to **block granularity** — after one LZ4 decompress of an SSTable block, run the predicate kernel over all rows' predicate columns (combined with existing zone maps to skip whole blocks), collect survivor offsets, then decode projected columns only for survivors. Longer term: PAX-style mini-column layout *inside* SSTable blocks so predicate-column bytes are contiguous (keeps the row-KV API, changes only block encoding — same spirit as TiDB's chunk RFC). Payoff scales with table width and predicate selectivity; near-zero payoff for `SELECT *` unfiltered scans, so do Step 1 first.

## Step 3: Morsel-driven parallelism replacing collect-then-rayon

- **Technique**: Fixed-size morsels (~100k rows; DuckDB parallelizes at 122,880-row row-group granularity) pulled by a worker pool with work stealing; degree of parallelism elastic at runtime, not baked into the plan. Leis et al., SIGMOD'14 (https://db.in.tum.de/~leis/papers/morsels.pdf); DuckDB's implementation (https://duckdb.org/docs/current/guides/performance/how_to_tune_workloads, https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/6632).
- **Applicability to FusionDB — MEDIUM-HIGH**: current parallelism (`scan/mod.rs` rayon `into_par_iter` at ~line 2383/2451) materializes all rows then filters in parallel — peak-memory heavy and no early-exit. FusionDB's LSM gives natural morsel boundaries: SSTable data-block ranges per level, with memtable deltas merged per-range; OCC snapshot reads mean morsels scan lock-free. Benefits: load balance across skewed key ranges, LIMIT early-termination across workers, and it composes with Steps 1–2 (a morsel = a few column batches). This generalizes the existing parallel range-merge rather than replacing it.

## What to SKIP: adaptive/JIT query compilation

- Kersten et al., VLDB'18 (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol11/p2209-kersten.pdf) — the definitive head-to-head: vectorized interpretation ≈ data-centric compilation on scan-heavy OLAP; compilation wins mainly on complex expression-heavy/OLTP-ish workloads. PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT experience shows tens-to-hundreds of ms compile latency that only pays off on long queries (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/jit-reason.html; empirical study https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.04692). For a Rust engine with no mature JIT story, ROI is poor. DataFusion (Rust, SIGMOD'24, https://andrew.nerdnetworks.org/pdf/SIGMOD-2024-lamb.pdf) reaches DuckDB-competitive performance with **zero JIT** — pure Arrow-batch vectorized streaming — the existence proof for the Rust path.
- **Cheap adaptivity to adopt instead**: Velox-style runtime conjunct reordering — score each filter by `time / (1 + values_in - values_out)`, evaluate best-dropping filter first (Velox paper above); DuckDB gets similar wins from optimizer-level filter pushdown alone, up to 30x (https://duckdb.org/2024/11/14/optimizers, https://motherduck.com/blog/announcing-duckdb-13-on-motherduck-cdw/). Trivially portable to FusionDB's predicate list in `scan/predicate.rs`.

## Recommended sequence

1. **Batch-columnar scan kernels** (Step 1) — attacks the dominant per-row `Value` decode+dispatch cost; CockroachDB/TiKV prove the pattern on identical architecture; expected order-of-magnitude on aggregate scans.
2. **Block-level predicate-first + survivor-only decode** (Step 2) — extends existing `decode_predicate_first_filtered_row` and zone maps; multiplies with Step 1 on selective/wide-table queries.
3. **Morsel scheduler** (Step 3) — replaces collect-then-rayon; needed to keep Steps 1–2 scaling across cores and to make LIMIT/early-exit work under parallelism.
4. Adaptive filter reordering as a low-cost bonus; defer JIT indefinitely.
